prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 1,200 words of the Apollo 13 accident and the crew's return to Earth. The reader is a general reader.

Do not use colons.

text:
On the afternoon of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted off from Florida carrying three men toward the Moon. Apollo 13 was meant to be the third lunar landing, and by then the public had begun to treat such journeys as routine. Jim Lovell, the commander, was the most experienced spaceflyer alive, a veteran of three earlier missions. Fred Haise would pilot the lunar module. The third seat belonged to Jack Swigert, a late replacement. Ken Mattingly, the original command module pilot, had been grounded just days before launch after exposure to German measles. He never actually caught the illness, but the doctors would not take the chance.

The first two days passed quietly. The crew named their command module Odyssey and their lunar module Aquarius. They sent home a television broadcast, giving viewers a tour of the cabin, and signed off to a public that was largely unimpressed. Networks did not carry it. Then, on the evening of April 13, about 56 hours into the flight and roughly 200,000 miles from Earth, Mission Control asked Swigert to flip a switch that stirred the supercold oxygen and hydrogen stored in the service module. The stirring was routine housekeeping that kept the tanks from stratifying and giving false readings.

Moments after Swigert threw the switch, a loud bang shook the spacecraft. Swigert reported, in the famously calm vocabulary of test pilots, that they had a problem. Lovell repeated it for the benefit of the ground. Warning lights lit across the panel. Voltage on one electrical bus dropped. The crew could see gas venting into space through the window, a steady glittering stream that would not stop.

What had happened was later traced to a chain of small errors that began years earlier. Oxygen tank number two had been damaged on the ground during a routine test, and the thermostat switches inside it had been fried by a higher voltage than they were built to survive. Nobody caught it. When Swigert stirred the tank, a spark from the damaged wiring ignited the Teflon insulation inside the pure oxygen. The pressure surged and the tank burst, blowing off an entire panel of the service module and crippling the neighboring tank too.

In Houston, flight director Gene Kranz gathered his teams in what the controllers called the Trench. The service module supplied the command module with power, water and breathing oxygen, and all of it was draining away. Within hours the fuel cells would be dead, and the command module would have only its entry batteries, which were meant for the final hour of the trip home. Landing on the Moon was already out of the question. The only goal now was survival.

The answer lay in the lunar module still attached to the nose of the stack. Aquarius had been designed to support two men for roughly two days on the Moon's surface. Now it would need to keep three men alive for four days, as a lifeboat. Lovell and Haise moved into it and began powering it up, while Swigert shut down Odyssey piece by piece to save what little energy it had left.

Next came the problem of the route. Apollo 13 had been aimed along a path that would have returned the ship to Earth had the engine failed, but days earlier mission planners had shifted it off that safe path to reach the intended landing site. Now the ship had to be steered back. Controllers considered turning around at once, but this would have meant using the service module engine, which no one trusted. Instead they chose to swing around the far side of the Moon and let its gravity slingshot the ship home. A burn of the lunar module's descent engine corrected the course. A second burn after the ship passed the Moon sped the return by hours. On the far side the crew reached a distance from Earth of nearly 250,000 miles, farther than any human beings have ever been before or since.

Then the lifeboat began to fail in smaller ways. The lunar module was never built to carry so many people for so long, and carbon dioxide slowly built up in the cabin. The cartridges that scrubbed the air in the lunar module were running out. The spare cartridges from the command module were square, while the lunar module sockets were round. Engineers on the ground, working with the same items the crew had aboard, devised an adapter from plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual, a sock, and a great deal of duct tape. They read the instructions up to the crew, who built it in their cabin, and the carbon dioxide readings fell back to a safe level. It remains one of the most celebrated improvisations in the history of engineering.

The days that followed were miserable. With almost no power, the cabin temperature sank to around freezing, and moisture condensed on the walls. The men slept little and ate cold food. They rationed water to a few ounces a day, and Haise developed a fever and a painful infection. Lovell later said the hardest thing was staying awake long enough to do the work. All the while the ship's alignment drifted, and without its computer fully running, the crew had to steer by hand, holding the Earth in the window of the spacecraft to keep the burn on target. Haise and Lovell managed a long manual burn exactly as the ground had calculated.

Meanwhile Mattingly, the astronaut who missed the flight, worked in a simulator on the ground with engineers to write a new procedure for restarting the command module with the tiny reserve of battery power available. Normally such a start-up took hours of careful steps and ample power. He had to find a way to do it using far less, and he did. The checklist went up to the crew on the final day.

On April 17 the crew set up for the end of the journey. They jettisoned the damaged service module first, and as it drifted away they finally saw how badly it had been wrecked, with a whole side torn open and debris trailing from it. Then they separated from Aquarius, which had saved them, and said goodbye to it. Odyssey, cold and dark, was the only ship left.

Reentry brought one more anxious stretch. The radio blackout caused by superheated air around the capsule normally lasted about three minutes. The seconds stretched on past that, with the controllers listening in silence to static, afraid the heat shield had been damaged by the explosion. At last Swigert's voice came through, and the capsule appeared beneath three red and white parachutes. It splashed down in the South Pacific near the recovery ship Iwo Jima, almost six days after launch.

The crew returned weary, thinner and unshaven, but unharmed. A review board concluded that the accident came from the tank's earlier damage and from design choices that had left it vulnerable, and NASA redesigned the tanks and the wiring. Lovell never did reach the Moon, though he had flown there twice. Apollo went on to land men on the Moon in several later missions, but the accident left behind something larger than a failed mission. It showed what a team of people on the ground and in space could do when everything went wrong, and it is remembered less as a failure than as a rescue.
